turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. It's really nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. 

Um... well, I hope I'm not wasting your time by being here. I know everyone gets a little overwhelmed with work sometimes, right? But I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I just... I can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. 

I have all these different things going on—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—and I try to keep on top of it, I really do. But I feel a little embarrassed to admit that lately, I just end up starting whatever is loudest instead of what actually matters. 

I hope that makes sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information to start with.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot organize the moving parts of their work and end up starting whatever is loudest instead of prioritizing what matters.

turns.doctor_question: Has this difficulty with organizing your tasks and staying focused on priorities been something you've struggled with since childhood, or is this a newer problem for you?
turns.patient_response:
Um... well, I suppose if I'm being completely honest, it's not entirely new. I mean, I was always a good kid, I promise! But... looking back, I guess some of this was there in grade school, too. 

My teachers always wrote that I was bright, which was really nice of them to say, but... they usually added that I daydreamed a bit. And, um, I feel a little silly admitting this at my age, but I used to forget to turn in my assignments. Like, I would actually finish the work, but then I'd just... lose my homework folders. And that was long before I was even a teenager. 

I hope that's not too much irrelevant detail? Is that the kind of timeline you were asking about?

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the difficulty with organization and focus, do you find that you spend a significant amount of your day worrying about a wide variety of different events or activities in your life?
turns.patient_response:
Um... well, no, I wouldn't say I worry all day. I mean, I definitely get a little stressed when I drop the ball on things, which I think is pretty normal, right? Like, anyone would feel a bit anxious if they forgot a deadline or lost an important paper. 

But it's not like I'm sitting around worrying about everything in my life. It's really just... the frustration of not being able to keep my ducks in a row. I try to stay positive and not let it get to me too much. 

I hope that answers your question? I just want to make sure I'm giving you an accurate picture. I'm not a super anxious person, I promise!

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel like you have a restless energy that makes it difficult for you to stay seated or remain still for long periods, such as during meetings or while working?
turns.patient_response:
Um... I guess I wouldn't call it restless energy, exactly. I mean, I don't want you to think I'm bouncing off the walls or anything disruptive like that. I'm usually pretty good at keeping it together! 

But... well, sometimes during those really long design calls—you know, the ones that just seem to drag on?—I do start to feel this sort of... pressure building up in my body. Like I just really, really need to stand up. 

I try to hide it, of course. I'll just, um, quietly pace around my home office a bit, or maybe just shift from one chair to another while I'm trying to look like I'm still paying close attention to the screen. It's just a little way to stretch my legs, I suppose. 

Is that... is that the kind of thing you mean? I hope I'm not making it sound worse than it is. I'm really not trying to be difficult or anything!

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a physical pressure building up in their body and a strong urge to stand up during long meetings, which indicates feelings of restlessness.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself blurting out answers before questions are completed, or do you frequently interrupt others while they are speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Um... no, no, I really don't think I do that. I try very hard to be polite and, you know, let people finish their thoughts. I mean, nobody likes being interrupted, right? 

I might get a little eager sometimes if we're brainstorming a really exciting software solution, but... I always try to wait my turn to speak. I definitely don't just blurt things out or talk over people. I'd feel terrible if I made anyone feel like I wasn't listening to them. 

So, um, no, I don't think that's really an issue for me. I hope that's a good thing? I really do try to be a good listener.

turns.doctor_question: When you are in situations that require you to stay quiet for a long time, do you find it difficult to keep your mind focused on what is being said, or do you find that your mind tends to wander off to other things?
turns.patient_response:
Um... well, yes, I suppose my mind does wander a bit. But I think everyone's mind wanders during long meetings, right? It's just human nature when you're sitting there for an hour or two. 

I mean, I really do try to pay attention. But sometimes, like during these big architecture meetings... someone will ask me a direct question, and I'll realize that I heard the first few words, but then... well, my brain just kind of drifted off into thinking about some specific implementation detail. 

It's actually a good thing in a way, because I'm thinking about the work! But then I have to ask them to repeat the question, which is a little embarrassing. I always apologize, of course, and say I was just caught up in the technical side of things. 

Does that sound like what you mean? I hope it doesn't make me sound like I don't care about what my team is saying. I really value their input, I just... get a little sidetracked by the work sometimes. Is that okay?

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood, would you say that the difficulty with staying focused and organized was much more prominent than any physical restlessness or tendency to act before thinking?
turns.patient_response:
Um... yes, I think that's a very fair way to put it. I was never really a hyper kid, you know? I wasn't getting into trouble or running around the classroom. I always tried to be a good student. 

But, well, if I'm being completely honest... looking back at grade school, those focus issues were definitely there. Even before I was a teenager. I remember my teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright—which was nice of them to say!—but that I daydreamed a lot. 

And, um, I did have this terrible habit of doing my homework and then... just forgetting to turn it in. Or I'd somehow lose my whole homework folder between my house and my desk. It wasn't that I didn't want to do the work, I just... couldn't seem to keep track of the papers. 

I feel a bit silly admitting that, a grown man talking about losing his homework in elementary school. But I suppose it's helpful for you to know, right? I just hope it doesn't make me sound irresponsible. I really did try my best to be organized, even back then!
